sentences.text: This extinct bird reached a total length of exactly 30 centimeters.
Its feathers displayed a pattern of white and grey mixed with darker brown and grey tones on the back, wings, and tail.
A distinctive feature was its long, slender, sharp, and frayed tongue, which likely moved rapidly to capture food.
The only known life drawing of this species was created by French artist Paul Philippe Sauguin de Jossigny in the early 1770s.
That same artist also produced the sole life drawing of the extinct Rodrigues parrot, suggesting he may have sketched the crested starling as well.
The earliest potential record comes from a list compiled in 1658 by French governor Étienne de Flacourt.
Early settlers on the island named these birds "huppe" because their crests and curved bills resembled those of hoopoes.
The bird likely lived in large groups within humid environments and marshlands.
It consumed both plant material and insects as part of its diet.
Anatomical features such as a robust pelvis, large feet, and strong jaws indicate it foraged close to the ground.
Analysis of stomach contents from a dissected specimen revealed seeds and berries from plants like Pseudobuxus and possibly Eugenia buxifolia.
Evidence suggests the species nested inside tree cavities.
Scientists propose that rising sea levels during the last interglacial period may have reduced its habitat, contributing to its population decline.
Taxonomically, the bird belongs to the kingdom Animalia, phylum Chordata, class Aves, order Passeriformes, family Sturnidae, and genus Fregilupus.
Boddaert originally named it Upupa varia, placing it in the hoopoe genus and translating the name as "mottled hoopoe" to describe its coloring.
In 1857, Hermann Schlegel argued the bird belonged to the starling family and reclassified it as Sturnus capensis.
The genus name Fregilupus was established by Lesson in 1831.
This species inhabited the island of Réunion and disappeared around the year 1850.
It lived throughout the Holocene epoch, spanning from 0.0117 to 0 million years ago.
Andrew John Berger questioned the bird's relationship with starlings in 1957, citing subtle anatomical differences.
While some authors suggested a link to vangas, Hiroyuki Morioka rejected this connection in 1996.
Various theories exist regarding its extinction, including competition, predation by introduced species, disease, deforestation, and human persecution for food or crop control.
Confusion persists regarding which physical characteristics were actually due to sexual dimorphism within the species.
